content: Dangerous goods training programs may require review and approval by the appropriate national authorities. Infectious substances, also referred to as infectious materials or products, are defined as microorganisms (such as bacteria, viruses, parasites, fungi) and other agents like prions that can cause disease in humans or animals. Before transporting any material, it is essential to determine whether it qualifies as an infectious substance. Cultures are biological agents intentionally propagated under controlled laboratory conditions in a designated medium or within animals. These concentrated collections of cultivated agents, known as cultures, are used in research, diagnostics, or stored in culture collections. Any cultured biological agent capable of causing disease in humans or animals is classified as an infectious substance. Patient specimens are materials collected directly from humans or animals for research or diagnostic purposes. These may include body fluids (e.g., excreta, secretions, blood, or blood products), tissues, or body parts collected in containers, on swabs, or preserved in media. If these specimens contain biological agents capable of causing disease, they are classified as infectious substances. Biological products are substances derived from living organisms (e.g., bacteria, fungi, vaccines, animals, humans) that are extracted or purified for use as preventive, therapeutic, or diagnostic tools. Examples include antitoxins, vaccines, or vaccine components. Due to their importance in disease treatment and prevention, some biological products may be subject to special requirements or licensing agreements set by national authorities. Their manufacture and distribution may also be regulated differently from infectious substances. Infected live animals that have been genetically modified or infected with biological agents must be transported according to the regulations of the country of origin, transit, and destination. These regulations typically focus on proper animal care, and infectious substance transport regulations generally do not apply. Live animals must not be used as a means to transport infectious substances unless no other method is feasible. Medical or clinical waste generated during patient treatment or laboratory activities may be contaminated with reagents, liquids, tissues, cultures, or other products. If this waste contains biological agents capable of causing disease, it is classified as an infectious substance. Medical waste containing Category A infectious substances must be assigned to UN 2814, UN 2900, or UN 3549, as appropriate. Solid medical waste containing Category A infectious substances from human or veterinary treatment may be assigned to UN 3549. However, this designation is not applicable for bioresearch waste or liquid waste. Category B infectious substances must be assigned to UN 3291. Waste believed to have a low probability of containing infectious substances should also be assigned to UN 3291, considering international, regional, or national waste catalogs. Medical devices or equipment contaminated with biological agents during patient treatment or laboratory processes may be classified as infectious substances if the agents can cause disease. Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) or microorganisms (GMMOs) that do not meet the definition of toxic or infectious substances must be assigned to UN 3245. COVID-19 vaccines containing GMOs or GMMOs, including those in clinical trials, are not subject to Dangerous Goods Regulations. For transport, materials defined as Exempt Human Specimens or Exempt Animal Specimens can be transported in a triple-layer packaging system without being subject to further infectious substance regulations. This packaging system includes a leak-proof primary receptacle, a leak-proof secondary container, and an outer packaging of sufficient strength. For liquids, absorbent material must be placed between the primary and secondary containers to prevent leakage. Used medical devices or equipment potentially contaminated with infectious substances must be packaged to prevent breakage, puncture, or leakage during transport. These packages must be marked as Used Medical Device or Used Medical Equipment. This exception does not apply to medical waste, devices contaminated with Category A infectious substances, or devices containing other hazardous materials. Classification of infectious substances involves determining whether the material reasonably contains biological agents capable of causing disease. If the material cannot be exempted, it is classified as an infectious substance. Classification must consider the material's composition and the level of risk it poses to human or animal health. Infectious substances are further categorized into Category A or Category B based on their potential to cause severe harm. These substances are assigned to UN 2814 (affecting humans) or UN 2900 (affecting animals only). The technical name of the hazardous biological agent must be included in parentheses after the proper shipping name on transport documents. Category B infectious substances are those that do not meet the criteria for Category A but still pose a risk. These are assigned to UN 3373 and labeled as Biological Substance, Category B. Medical or clinical waste containing Category B infectious substances must be assigned to UN 3291. For Category A substances, additional testing and approval processes are required to meet Packing Instruction P620. Packaging must be sourced from compliant manufacturers, and clear instructions for proper use must be provided.
